rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse echoes 4:110, where a wrongdoer who seeks God's forgiveness finds Him Forgiving and Merciful.
rows.anchor: This verse is similar to 4:110: Whosoever does evil or wrongs himself, and then seeks forgiveness of God

rows.speaker: many scholars
rows.claim: Many scholars count this among the Quran's most hopeful verses; the commentary also lists other hopeful verses and says some call these the most joyous.
rows.anchor: Many scholars consider this to be among the most hopeful verses of the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address is understood to encompass all humanity.
rows.anchor: Although this verse addresses all of humanity

rows.speaker: many commentators
rows.claim: Some understand the verse as first addressing Makkans who feared they could not repent and follow the Prophet after idolatry, invoking deities, unlawful killing, or fornication.
rows.anchor: many understand it to have initially addressed the situation of some Makkans who feared that they could not repent

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their prodigality covers every kind of sin, including killing innocent people in the pre-Islamic Age of Ignorance.
rows.anchor: Their being prodigal to the detriment of their own souls would then refer to all manner of sin

rows.speaker: other commentators
rows.claim: Another view says it was revealed about Muslims whom the Makkans barred from migrating to Madinah, persecuted into renouncing Islam, and who feared they could not repent.
rows.anchor: Others understand this verse to have been revealed in reference to a small group of Muslims whom the Makkans had prevented from migrating to Madinah

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: Thawbān reports that the Prophet valued this verse above the whole world and everything in it.
rows.anchor: According to Thawbān, a freed slave of the Prophet, the Prophet said, “I would not wish to have the entire world

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: When asked whether forgiveness could include someone who associates partners with God, the Prophet answered three times, “And why not?”
rows.anchor: The Prophet was silent and then said three times, “And why not one who associates partners with God?”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Forgiveness of idolatry depends on renouncing it and repenting, as 4:48 and 4:116 state that God does not forgive association of partners.
rows.anchor: Such forgiveness would, however, be contingent upon the renouncement of idolatry and repentance for it

rows.speaker: a third opinion
rows.claim: A third view says the verse corrects Muslims who believed every major sinner belonged to the people of the Fire.
rows.anchor: According to a third opinion, this verse was revealed to correct a group of Muslims who held that anyone who committed a major sin

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet says that if people did not sin and seek forgiveness, God would replace them with people who sin, seek forgiveness, and are forgiven.
rows.anchor: the Prophet said, “If you did not sin [and seek forgiveness], God would remove you and come with a people who would sin

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As at 39:18, following the most beautiful revelation does not rank one part above another; it means acting according to revelation through obedience and avoidance of disobedience.
rows.anchor: what is most beautiful of what God has revealed is not understood to mean that one part is more beautiful than another

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another formulation is to practice what God enjoins and avoid what He forbids; revelation achieves its purpose when its injunctions are put into practice.
rows.anchor: it is only when the injunctions contained in revelation have been put into practice that their purpose is achieved

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some understand the phrase to mean the Quran is the best or most beautiful of God's revealed books, as in 39:23.
rows.anchor: Some understand this verse to mean that the Quran is the best or most beautiful of the books that God has sent down

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning means that a person should not wait until it is too late before seeking repentance.
rows.anchor: Lest any soul should say, that is, lest anyone should seek to repent only when it is too late

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Alas for me expresses the utmost regret and grief for failing to perform God's enjoined deeds.
rows.anchor: Alas for me is understood as an expression of utmost regret and grief (R) for having failed to perform the deeds enjoined by God

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: The phrase rendered “of my duty to God” literally means “of” or “from the side of God” and can mean God's Right.
rows.anchor: which literally means “of” or “from the side of God” and is interpreted to mean, “of God’s Right”

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Other interpretations of the phrase are neglecting obedience to God or missing God's reward.
rows.anchor: “of obedience to God” (Q, Ṭs, Z), or “of the reward of God”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic janb, “side,” can suggest bodily, emotional, or spiritual closeness; the phrase may mean nearness to God or Paradise, nearness to what leads to Him, or seeking His nearness.
rows.anchor: can allude to physical, emotional, and spiritual closeness, as when one speaks of being by another’s side in English.

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: The scoffers are those who mocked the Quran and the Messenger.
rows.anchor: The scoffers are those who scoffed at the Quran and the Messenger

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: The lament can be correct in that God guides whomever He wills to a straight path.
rows.anchor: On the one hand, this lament is understood as correct (Q, R), since God guides whomsoever He will unto a straight path

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People remain responsible for not following God's guidance: He offered signs, but some refused to reflect, turned from the Quran, and pursued worldly vanities; God answers that His signs came to them.
rows.anchor: people are responsible for not having followed God’s guidance, for God offered signs, but some chose not to look at or reflect upon them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike the prior verse's blame of God, this soul acknowledges some culpability and asks for a second chance, as do the guilty in 32:12.
rows.anchor: those represented in this verse acknowledge some culpability and ask to be given a second chance, as in 32:12

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Such pleas are insincere and useless because revelation was given and respite lasted until death; even if returned, they would again do what they were forbidden, and are called liars in 6:28.
rows.anchor: such lamentations are not considered sincere and are of no avail, for even if they were sent back, they would return to the very thing they had been forbidden

rows.speaker: many commentators
rows.claim: Many understand “Call upon Me” as “Worship Me,” also supported by the following warning against arrogance about worship.
rows.anchor: Call upon Me, or “Supplicate unto Me,” is understood by many to mean, “Worship Me,” as when the Prophet said

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet says supplication is worship and recites this verse.
rows.anchor: as when the Prophet said, “Supplication is worship,” and then recited this verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the verse enjoins supplication to God, which itself implies worship; many Muslims follow the Prophet by supplicating after obligatory prayers.
rows.anchor: The verse can also be understood as an injunction to call upon God, which would itself imply worship

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's promise to respond does not mean every supplication is answered in this life.
rows.anchor: I shall respond to you is a promise from God, but it is not understood to mean that all supplications will be answered in this life

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAjībah
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAjībah says God grants the believer's request either in this life or stores it for the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: Ibn ʿAjībah writes, “There is no believer who calls upon God and asks Him for something but that God gives it to him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Supplication is meritorious because it humbly acknowledges servitude, abasement, poverty before God, and complete need of Him.
rows.anchor: Supplication is considered among the most meritorious of acts, because in humbly imploring God one admits to one’s servitude

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most who fail to call upon God do so from pride and arrogance.
rows.anchor: Thus most who fail to call upon God do so out of pride and arrogance

rows.speaker: ḥadīth qudsī
rows.claim: A famous sacred report says that one whose remembrance distracts from supplication receives something more bountiful than what is given to those who supplicate.
rows.anchor: For one whose remembrance of Me has distracted him from imploring Me, I shall give him that which is more bountiful

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentary points to its discussion of calling upon God at 2:186.
rows.anchor: for more on the importance of “calling upon God,” see 2:186c

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's reviving barren land is an argument for His ability to resurrect human beings, as in many other verses.
rows.anchor: This is one of several verses to invoke God’s ability to revive barren land as an argument for His ability to resurrect human beings

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: The revived land can symbolize a soul dried by heedlessness and ignorance, stirred by the water of life or wine of Divine Love and revived through God's remembrance and knowledge.
rows.anchor: is revived by the remembrance of God and knowledge of Him (Aj).

rows.speaker: al-Qushayrī
rows.claim: Al-Qushayrī reads the verse as a heart drawing near to God when humbled by awareness of sin and then displaying the blessings of regret and repentance.
rows.anchor: al-Qushayrī sees this verse as a metaphor for the condition of a heart to which God draws near

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening resembles 4:163–64; the Quran's treatment of revelation's universality is discussed in the essay on sacred history and other religions.
rows.anchor: The first part of this verse is similar to 4:163–64

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Upholding religion means acting in accord with it, or holding fast, fulfilling its obligations, remaining faithful, and calling others to it.
rows.anchor: To uphold religion means that to act in accord with it (Ṭ) or to hold fast to it, perform its obligations

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Avoiding division means not repeating earlier religious communities' sectarianism, but remaining united as brothers.
rows.anchor: to not be like earlier religious communities that divided into sects (Ṭ), but rather to remain united in religion as brothers (Ṭs).

rows.speaker: al-Ṭabarī
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī says division is destruction, while unity is something upon which one can rely.
rows.anchor: al-Ṭabarī says that division is destruction and being unified is something upon which one can rely

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: The call is grievous to idolaters because it undermines their religion and because they envy Muhammad for receiving revelation instead of someone else.
rows.anchor: The Prophet’s call to belief in Divine Unity and sincere devotion to God is grievous for the idolaters both because it undermines their religion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The antecedent of the pronoun rendered “Himself” is uncertain; the sentence can instead read that God chooses and guides whomever He wills “for it,” meaning religion or bearing witness to Divine Unity.
rows.anchor: The antecedent of the pronoun here rendered Himself is not completely clear. The sentence could also be read

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's guidance of whoever turns in repentance evokes a sacred report about God drawing nearer to the servant who draws near to Him.
rows.anchor: That God guides whosoever turns in repentance (cf. 13:27) evokes the famous ḥadīth qudsī

rows.speaker: ḥadīth qudsī
rows.claim: The sacred report says God responds to a servant's approach by drawing nearer, and comes running when the servant comes walking.
rows.anchor: if he comes to Me walking, I go to him running

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What is given in this world is its fleeting delight, described elsewhere as the enjoyment of delusion.
rows.anchor: Enjoyment of the life of this world indicates the ephemeral delights of this world, which are naught but the enjoyment of delusion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The world's ephemeral delights contrast with the more lasting rewards of the next life; the passage also refers to 28:60 and 29:64.
rows.anchor: which are more lasting; see 29:64c.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh idolaters acknowledged one God as creator but worshipped other deities alongside Him and denied resurrection.
rows.anchor: they acknowledged that one God was responsible for creation, but they nonetheless worshipped other deities alongside Him (IK) and denied His ability to resurrect (R).

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Alternatively, “them” and “they” refer to the prophets, all of whom affirm that God created the heavens and earth; on this reading, 43:10–13 may continue their quotation.
rows.anchor: Alternately, them and they can be understood as references to the prophets (R), meaning that all prophets affirm this statement.

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: The earth as a cradle means it is smooth and easy to travel upon.
rows.anchor: That God made the earth a cradle means He made the earth smooth, easy to travel upon

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: The earth is also made tractable for agriculture and a home for human life.
rows.anchor: tractable for agriculture (R), and a home for human life.

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: The paths are navigable routes God made upon the earth.
rows.anchor: refers to navigable routes He has made upon it (IK, JJ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In context, guidance means God facilitates earthly travel and provides signs and revelation leading to truth and Paradise in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: God both facilitates travel upon the earth in this life and provides signs and revelation to guide human beings to truth and to Paradise

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Water sent in due measure suffices to sustain people, livestock, and crops, and is not ordinarily a deluge like the flood in Noah's time.
rows.anchor: God sends water sufficient to sustain people, livestock, and crops (IK) and does not usually send down a deluge (JJ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran elsewhere says God created everything and measured it out; the theological significance of measure is discussed at 54:49.
rows.anchor: Elsewhere it is said that God created everything, then measured it out with due measure

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reviving dead land is used here and elsewhere as a metaphor for human resurrection.
rows.anchor: The last line of the present verse is one of several places where the Quran employs the revivification of dead land as a metaphor for the resurrection of human beings

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: The image also symbolizes the death and life of the soul.
rows.anchor: Such imagery is also understood as a spiritual allegory and symbol for the death and life of the soul

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: The pairs refer variously to all animal species, all opposites, or male and female members of animal kinds.
rows.anchor: refers to all species of animals (IK, Q), to all opposites (R), or to the fact that all animals have both males and females (Q).

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī argues that pairs show created things are relative and multiple, whereas their Creator is Absolute and transcends duality.
rows.anchor: According to al-Rāzī, that they are pairs indicates that they are all relative and multiple

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seafaring and cattle are blessings; cattle serve riding and transport, warmth and clothing, food and drink, and beauty as signs of God's beneficence.
rows.anchor: mention seafaring as a blessing bestowed by God (cf. 14:32; 17:66; 22:65; 30:46) and invoke the benefits of cattle

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslims commonly use this supplication when traveling by land; for sea travel, they are advised to use the prayer in 11:41.
rows.anchor: The supplication given at the end of this verse is often employed by Muslims when traveling by land

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Acknowledging that creation is made subservient to people, though they are not its equal, admits people cannot use these resources without Divine Aid.
rows.anchor: human beings do not have the capacity to make use of these resources without Divine Aid

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase may mean that people turn to their Lord in prayer, or alternatively that they return to Him in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: that is, in prayer. Alternately, the phrase could be rendered, “Unto our Lord do we return” in the Hereafter (Aj, IK,R, Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the Hereafter reading, earthly journeys recall the journey to the Hereafter, and travel provisions recall the need to prepare with reverence.
rows.anchor: mention of earthly journeys in the previous verse draws one’s attention to the journey toward the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The return after mentioning travel recognizes the dangers of setting out unprepared and that successful return depends entirely on God.
rows.anchor: recognition of the dangers inherent in setting out upon a journey, especially without the necessary preparation, and that the successful return from a journey lies entirely in God’s Hands

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The active participle munqalibūn makes the return definitive: all people travel toward God at every moment, whether willingly or not.
rows.anchor: “are we returners”) speaks to the definitive nature of this verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Leaders and notables usually resist messengers most because they benefit from a corrupt social order and stand to lose most from a just one; elsewhere they are called the guilty.
rows.anchor: the leaders or notables of a community who are usually most adamant in opposing God’s messengers, implying that they benefit from a corrupt social order

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentary cites leaders' opposition to Moses, Noah, other prophets, and Muhammad across multiple passages.
rows.anchor: It is the leaders and notables who are said to have opposed Moses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disbelievers treat following their forefathers as sufficient justification for their beliefs and actions.
rows.anchor: implies that they see following the ways of their forefathers as sufficient justification for their beliefs and actions
